idiom_name: pooled SocketAsyncEventArgs completion loop (async/await) on the runtime's I/O thread pool
implementation_notes: The .NET base class library has no leader/follower type; the runtime occupies the demultiplexing role instead. Asynchronous socket operations are completed by the platform's I/O completion machinery and dispatched on the thread pool, so the high-throughput shape is a preallocated pool of SocketAsyncEventArgs objects - one outstanding receive per socket, a shared buffer manager, and a Semaphore bounding accepted clients - rather than a set of threads rotating a leadership token; the completion dispatcher holds that role permanently. Task-based async/await over the same primitives is the everyday form. Socket.Select is the manual route: it poll-checks a socket list on the calling thread, which is the only way to own the readiness set when the application must inspect it itself, and it must not be mixed with outstanding asynchronous operations on the same sockets.
pitfalls: Reusing or recycling a SocketAsyncEventArgs before its pending operation completes corrupts that operation; the pool may only be refilled from the completion callback.
Socket.Select owns the wait set: sockets polled through it must have no asynchronous operation outstanding, and two threads calling it with the same list double-report readiness.
Blocking inside a completion callback, or in library async code without ConfigureAwait(false), starves the thread pool that dispatches every other socket.
An exception thrown in the completion callback is swallowed by the infrastructure if it is not handled, leaving the socket silently dead.
